report:
**Conclusion: yes.** High-quality randomized evidence shows that denosumab (Prolia) lowers the risk of *new vertebral fractures* in postmenopausal women with osteoporosis.

The pivotal FREEDOM trial was a large, randomized, placebo-controlled trial (7,868 women). Participants received denosumab 60 mg under the skin every six months or placebo for 36 months. Denosumab significantly reduced vertebral, hip, and nonvertebral fractures. [https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/nejmoa0809493](https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/nejmoa0809493)

For vertebral fractures specifically, the FDA label reports 3-year rates of **2.3% with Prolia versus 7.2% with placebo**: an absolute reduction of **4.8 percentage points** and a **68% relative risk reduction** (statistically significant, p<0.0001). Put another way, roughly 1 new radiographic vertebral fracture was prevented for every 21 women treated for three years in this trial population. [https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/label/2012/125320s0078lbl.pdf](https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/label/2012/125320s0078lbl.pdf)

Important context: this direct fracture-outcome evidence is strongest for postmenopausal women with osteoporosis, and benefit depends on receiving injections on schedule. Denosumab should not simply be stopped or substantially delayed without a clinician’s plan for follow-on osteoporosis treatment, because vertebral fractures can occur after discontinuation. [https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/label/2025/125320s219lbl.pdf](https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/label/2025/125320s219lbl.pdf)
